content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper is about a representation of high-level skills for sequential decision making contexts (in this particular paper: planning-based based on full models, instead of reinforcement learning). The idea is to take a "next"-based representation in which high-level skills can be put in order in a task. Each skill is characterized by (learned) functions predicting whether a state either supports the initialisation or the termination of a skill, and tasks are accompanied by simple automate over skills. Several variations of planning (A*/IDA variants) and methods for learning the two mentioned functions are covered. Experiments in two domains are performed against related baselines.
content.main_review:
The fields of planning, robotics, reinforcement learning etc have a huge history when it comes to abstractions over action sequences (skills, options, high-level actions, abstract actions, etc). This paper is positioned somewhere in this field, and uses a simple automata-based representation of task in terms of skills (with a "before" ordering) and two functions for precondition and termination checking. Learning them is based on data that consists of sequences of actions and the high-level task structure. The paper defines several tasks (planning with skills, planning with one goal condition, and inverse planning). I do not think that there is much technically wrong with the paper, although some things are unclear (see below), and I also think the experiments show viability results, but my main issue with the paper is novelty/significance of the approach compared to the vast literature on actions. Basically I do not see a clear contribution compared to the literature, but I do see a (in essence fairly useful) mix of existing methods that seems to work well for these problems (although the experiments raise some questions, see below). Overall I have several questions which need to be answered too. In addition, the paper is written fairly well, although it contains some small things like typos. I will elaborate (and mix that with questions I have).

- First of all: why call it "rational" skills? First of all, "RAT"skills may not sound nice. But more importantly, the rational here is relatively meaningless. I think what is meant here, is "reasonable", or "relatively fault-free", or "believable". Throughout the paper rational means that, for example, the data contains trajectories that have not been generated randomly, but are close to regular or optimal trajectories. Is that right? If right, I would more clearly talk about these other aspects.
- The introduction is ok, but why not frame it in existing formalisms such as "options", which are well-known in reinforcement learning, and come with aspects such as states where the option (skill) is applicable/terminating. Many papers have built on this, and hierarchical planning methods exist too.
- The related work description contains many papers, but the positioning of the paper is weak. Modular skill models are described, and they contain things like LTL, but this paper is much simpler than the usual setting there. The paper only uses a simple automaton with a temporal structure (next-based) for tasks to endow the current (real) state with the current skill being executed. Hierarchical RL (and planning), which is also used in robotics, would have to get much more focus and description than now; there is much more related literature in this field. Even more so since several HRL techniques learn skills and decompositions while learning, for example by finding "bottleneck states", "subgoal discovery", or milestones, which can be used for delineation of tasks from data. Furthermore, I think that there is also lots of related work in the area of "activity recognition", since what the paper does (segmenting an action sequence, and putting labels on segments) is technically the same. Inverse planning is described briefly, but activity and behavior recognition would be relevant too. Also, I think that work in the general field of Hidden Markov Models for such tasks is relevant. Basically the paper utilizes similar methods for segmenting the task and learning predictors for precondition/termination, just like HMMs can use neural networks to induce latent labels. Finally, I would also expect maybe algorithms like dynamic time warping (DTW) to be mentioned since using dynamic programming for this alignment is known. I am not saying everything needs to be mentioned in this form, but I do think the positioning especially wrt hierarchical reinforcement learning and planning is not well done.
- Why focus on deterministic processes (Section 3.1 first line) while many other, related methods, in this field cover stochastic environments? Where does this limitation come from exactly?
- Neural Logic Machine are mentioned, but never explained in the paper. In fact, only some words reveal that (some form of) neural networks are used for learning, but the details of how, and why, are completly undescribed.
- There is some abuse of notation on page 3 when going from actions to sequences of actions, which is ok, but can be better described.
- I like the idea of models vs learning policies (last sentence of page 3) but I am not sure that for all environments full plans can be generated, especially when things are computed online, or if there is uncertainty at play.
- There is some confusion about the execution of skills. The text says things about "interleaving", but the formalism seems to enforce strict orders (and completion of skills), for example in Figure 2, but also later (page 4) "indicate THE skill" and "executing THE current skill". If you still insist that skills can be run in parallel, please specify how, and also how many can run in parallel.
- How is lambda chosen? In addition, the motivation behind the definition of C' sounds ok, but the technical implementation needs more description for me. In the definition, do you mean/assume that v and v' are not equal?
- The sentence starting with "The finite state..." occurs twice(!)
- The first two tasks on page 5/6 sound like standard planning problems, which is interesting in general, but if there is a contribution here, please specify.
- The Bayesian inverse planning is not well motivated or explained. It looks like standard approaches ranging from related inverse planning, to HMM-like methods, to DTW, and so on. If there is a contribtion, please specify.
- The text mentions that Fig 3 shows the value function, but I have not idea what it means here or what I can see in it.
- What is the "score" in the rationality definition? And how does this definition relate to standard Boltzmann/softmax action selection and so on?
- The section on learning the ratskills needs much more explanation on how this objective is actually learned in the neural logic machines, and also why it makes sense to do it exactly like this. The text assumes the reader knows ("since") that the functions are differentiable, but this is nowhere introduced yet. Some things like "running back-propagation through the inverse planning" do not make sense to me.
- For the experimental section, some baselines are introduced, but it is hard to find out that this is the actual state-of-the-art in this domain, or for these problems. This is made worse by the weak positioning of the work.
- The results in the tables seem to be very favourable for the method that is described, but even for the planning tasks the competing methods perform very weak, which seems strange. I have no idea whether this makes sense (Table 1).
- I think it is fairly confusing how the "compositional" and "novel" tasks are described and what they actually mean. 
- I think one of the main results could be the sentence on page 8 "learning goals from demonstrations is more sample-efficient than learning policies". This sounds intuitive, and could be true. However, I do think it is also related to the deterministic nature of the problems considered.
- The result for the planning problems sound ok, but I have difficulties finding out the relation to the SOTA, but the final experiments on inverse planning are inconclusive to me. Overall, the experiments are not intuitively structured (for me at least). I think more targeted experimentation, with more clear goals, would be helpful. Now all settings, including learning, and the primitive, compositional, and novel tasks are all somewhat mixed up.
content.summary_of_the_review: A mix of methods in the action domain, mixing some high-level skill representation, deterministic planning, and some skill learning with behavioral segmentation from data, but it is unclear where the paper is positioned in a huge field of action-related papers (affecting contributions, novelty and significance), and the experiments are somewhat inconclusive. Technically, I think the paper is mostly sound, fairly well written. In addition, there are several things that are not fully described yet.

content.title: Author Response to Reviewer jHeZ - part 1
content.comment:
Thank you for your helpful comments.

**Q1:** Why call it "rational skills" instead of reliable? Why not frame them as options?

**A:** The notion of rational skill concepts is fundamentally different from options in the following ways. And this is also why we call them "rational" instead of "reliable".
1. The terminal conditions of options are similar to the goal conditions of rational skill concepts, but they are used differently at execution time.
2. Executing an option is fundamentally different from executing a skill concept. An option has a policy that we can follow to achieve the short-term goal. Skill concepts should be refined with segments of primitives that complete them, following the principle of "global rationality": i.e., the agent is minimizing the overall cost of the task instead of a sequence of short-term goals. In some cases, the execution of skills may interleave -- some skills can be completed while the agent is also making progress towards other skills (Figure 7 in Appendix A provides an example).
3. The initial condition $I_t$ in our setting also limits the horizon of planning. For example, our planning algorithm will not try to plan for "holding an axe" (the subgoal for skill "pickup-axe") if we haven't yet built an axe (because the initial condition for "pickup-axe" -- having an axe on the ground -- is not satisfied).

---

**Q2:** Position of this paper (compared to modular skill models, Hierarchical RL, activity recognition, HMM tasks, and DTW)

**A:** HMMs and other activity recognition approaches focus on learning to understand tasks, which may also require task segmentation. Compared to them, RatSkills focuses on acquiring models that can be used not only for activity recognition, but also for planning, both to complete specified task descriptions but also to plan when only the terminal goal condition is specified.

As for task segmentation, HMMs are based on the hypothesis that actions within a segment are similar (follow the same distribution). In contrast, Ratskills are based on the hypothesis that actions within a segment are rational sequences intended to achieve the same goal.  Crucially, the particular actions generated by the same Ratskill may be quite different from execution to execution, becase they depend on detail both on the state from which they are being executed and on the requirements of the other subtasks in the overall specification.

Regarding DTW, we agree that our dynamic programming is similar to warping trajectories into sequential skills, but we compute the "cost" at each segment instead of each pair of matched positions. We have included a discussion of this in the revised paper.

---

**Q3:** Why focus on deterministic processes?

In this first paper, to allow us to focus on the novel Ratskill formulation of learning hierarchical skill models, we assume that there is a good deterministic approximation to the actual underlying world dynamics.  Our learning approach is robust to the case in which the demonstration sequences exhibit some deviations from the assumed world dynamics, because our objective $J_t$ depends on whether the actions selected by the agent in each state are rational given the model, but is unaffected by world transitions in which $s_{i+1}$ is not the expected outcome of action $a$ in state $s_i$.

In a domain with moderate stochasticity, approaches based on planning with a deterministic approximation, embedded in a feedback loop that observes the world state and replans as necessary, can be very effective, and our current methods would be applicable in such cases.  In domains where the stochasticity is substantial, and especially in which the downside risk of low-probability outcomes must be taken into account (e.g., the demonstrator takes the "long way around" in order to avoid a small chance of falling into a hole), the high-level concepts of Ratskills could be retained (defining rationality of a state/action subsequence relative to an objective) but significant algorithmic changes would be required both in training and execution.

---

**Q4:** Neural logical machine.

**A:** Neural Logical Machines are a neural symbolic architecture for logical relational reasoning and can be trained via SGD.  They could have been replaced in this work by graph neural networks extended to have higher-arity relations (e.g., hyper-graph NNs).  An architecture of this type is necessary to be able to generalize to problems with different numbers of objects, locations, etc.
NLM can implicitly realize first order logic to model relations, such as: "The agent is holding an axe" ($\exists x. $ is_axe $(x) \land $ held $(x)$), "The agent is standing on a cell with a crafting table" ($\exists x. $ is_crafting_table $(x)\land $agent_at$ (x)$).

---

content.comment:
**Q5:** Generating full plan may be unrealistic.

**A:** We agree that generating the full plan may be unrealistic for long-horizon problems in stochastic environments.  As discussed above, many stochastic environments can be addressed effectively using replanning relative to a determinized model, but in a highly stochastic domain, frequent recomputation of a full plan may be very expensive.  In such circumstances, a truly hierarchical approach, in which a detailed plan is only made for a shorter-horizon prefix of the task sequence might be an effective approach.


---

**Q6:** Interleave skills.

**A:** Executing rational skills via planning allows us to optimize the overall cost of the task instead of the short-term sub-goal. Sometimes interleaving is needed to achieve such "global rationality". Figure 7 in Appendix A provides a concrete example where such interleaving is necessary for the optimal trajectory. 

---

**Q7:** Details in technique implementation.

**A:** Ideally $G_v(s)=0$ when $s$ is not completed, so the value of $\lambda$ doesn't matter, because invalid transitions can never be made. In practice, we use a softer version to avoid invalid transitions. Typically we don't want the agent to perform an undesired transition when $G_v(s)$ is low (say $0.1$). $\lambda$ is chosen also based on the average (or worst case) cost to complete a single skill, so taking many actions to complete the skill is worth the cost. In practice, we choose $\lambda=1$ because each skill in the worst case costs less than $2$, and $-\lambda \cdot \log (0.1) \approx 2.3>2$.

In addition, we assume $v \neq v'$.

---

**Q8:** Planning tasks.

**A:** The key difference in our setting is that the agent does not get any reward signal from the environment; i.e., it doesn't know whether a task or a sub-task is completed. It is very common that the physical world does not provide any explicit signal in reality. The agent needs to infer this information using its learned skill representations. Other aspects of our planning problems are indeed standard.

---

**Q9:** Bayesian inverse planning.

**A:** To explain the motivation of using inverse planning, we need to point out that in our setting the agent does not get any reward signal from the environment during both training and testing. The agent does not know what "grab the axe" means, and the environment does not tell it whether "grab the axe" has been completed. All this knowledge is learned by inferring the intention of rational agents performing the demonstrations with Bayesian inverse planning.

In addition, we extend inverse planning to incorporate FSMs to learn from tasks with temporal structures and plan for them, which we mark as a contribution. For contributions on modeling and generalizing to temporally structured tasks, please refer to our general response.



---

**Q10:** Value function in Fig 3.

**A:** Fig 3 is a visualization of a $J_t$ function, where $J_t$ estimates the cost to complete the whole task from the current state $s$ and FSM node $v$. A deeper color means a larger cost. For example, at the node "craft a boat", the closer the agent is to the boat station, the smaller the cost. At the node "collect wood", the agent needs first to go to the tree to collect wood and then go to the boat station to craft the boat. Hence the cost is the distance between the agent and the tree plus the distance between the tree and the boat station. The plot for the "mine gold" node is similar. Finally, at the starting node $v_0$, the agent has two choices to complete the task, and a rational agent chooses the one with a smaller cost based on its initial location. Hence, taking the element-wise minimum of the $J_t$ values at the "collect wood" and "mine gold" nodes leads to the values on node $v_0$. We will emphasize that $J_t$ is a value function that estimates the cost in our revision.

---

**Q11:** The definition of rationality score?

**A:** Note that the $Rat$ term in the rationality score is a standard likelihood with respect to a Boltzmann/softmax action-selection distribution along the trajectory. Besides the standard Boltzmann distribution, we additionally focus on whether each sub-goal (skill) is completed when the corresponding transition is performed. We observed that the rationality $Rat$ cannot be well estimated when the agent is far from the goal, and adding the $\log G_v(s_i) +\log I_{v'}(s_i)$ terms can help learning. 

---

content.comment:
**Q12:** How and why RatSkills are learned?

**A:** Each skill is represented by an initial condition and a goal condition, realized by NLMs. As we mentioned, NLMs can model lifted logical rules using normal neural operators (such as tensor pooling), and are fully differentiable. $J_t$ are computed based on $I_t$ and $G_t$ using Bellman-Ford (thus differentiable w.r.t. the network weights), and rationality scores and the loss functions are computed from $J_t$ (thus also differentiable w.r.t. the network weights), so the framework is thoroughly differentiable -- the standard back-propagation can optimize the parameter of $I_t/G_t$ (realized by NLMs) by minimizing the loss.

---

**Q13:** Are baselines the state-of-the-art in this domain?

**A:** The problem we are solving is *new*, and our key contribution is learning the goal-centric representation. First, we are unaware of any similar methods that also learn goal-centric representations as we do and do planning. Second, thus, we have adapted baselines for learning reward (IRL) and learning policies (behavior cloning) into our task.


---

**Q14:** Performance in table 1.

**A:** Compared to behavior cloning methods that directly apply a learned policy, our model runs A*/RRT search based on the learned goal classifier. This suggests that learning goals from demonstrations is more sample-efficient than learning policies, and generalizes better to new maps. Meanwhile, compared with IRL methods, our task representation composed by goal-centric skills has more compositional structure and thus performs better in these domains.

---

**Q15:** What do "compositional" and "novel" mean?

**A:** "Compositional" means the tasks may consist of more than one skill connected by $\textbf{and}, \textbf{or},$ and $\textbf{then}$. In our experiment setting, tasks in the compositional split are seen during training. The novel split contains 12 composite tasks containing more skills than the compositional split, but they were never seen during training.

---

**Q16:** Learning goals rather than policies, and the deterministic nature of the problem.

**A:** Our framework does generalize to non-deterministic environments.  If there is mild non-determinism, it can be used directly, and understood as learning a deterministic approximation in a stochastic domain.  At execution time, it would be necessary to monitor the resulting states and replan if necessary.   If there is more substantial non-determinism, then the same principles would apply, but some techniques would have to change, such as using value iteration rather than Bellman-Ford, and using MCTS rather than $A^*$ for planning.  This extension would be conceptually straightforward but not trivial to implement.

---

**Q17:** How is the experiment structured?

**A:** In our general response, we have stated the advantages of our framework: (1)improving planning efficiency and creating language interfaces for (2) trajectory description and (3) instruction following. Thus, our three experiments directly target these three tasks.

**Planning for tasks with descriptions.** We focus on using the learned skills for planning and illustrate this as a measurement of how effective RatSkills are for planning tasks. These experiments also demonstrate our ability to plan for novel compositional tasks. Compared to the planning settings in hierarchical planning papers including Hierarchical RL, the **reward function is not available** in the environment.

**Planning for tasks with black-box tests.** This shows that our learned skill representations can help search for plans, assuming that the task is achievable within short skill sequences. We first search for task candidates composed by skills, and then search plans for these task candidates. This hierarchical search does make the planning more efficient even when using blind search. A theoretical justification can be found in our general response.

This approach is also easily combined with any learned/hand-crafted heuristic, but learning heuristics is not the focus of our paper. 

**Inverse planning.** Though we do not state activity recognition as a novel contribution, we provide the results on inverse planning to ensure that our learning with Bayesian inverse planning is successful, and RatSkills also have the ability to recognize seen and novel tasks.

---

**Minor edit suggestions:** Thanks for your suggestions and we have revised our paper accordingly.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper looks at the problem of learning skills from annotated traces, which can then be used for planning and task identification. In particular, the paper looks at plan traces annotated with a task specification, which is provided in a task language introduced in the paper that the authors argue to be a subset of LTL. The language consists of strings that are recursively constructed from a set of atomic skills and some connectives. Each atomic skill is defined in terms of an initiation state set and termination state set, each operationalized by using classifiers for each set. They use a contrastive learning method to learn the classifiers for the initiation and termination set and discuss how the learned skills could be used for planning and task identification. The planning makes use of an augmented state space, where each task state is augmented with finite state machine states that captures the progress of the task execution. The planning and inverse planning performance of the system is evaluated on two tasks and compared against an IRL-based and a behavior cloning-based baseline. They additionally consider an LSTM based classification method for task identification. The initial results seem to be positive and show their method outperforming the baselines.
content.main_review:
I think the paper looks at an interesting and important problem. Being able to take input from people in a natural way is an important capability for autonomous agents. Also as pointed out by the paper itself, procedural control knowledge of the form is particularly useful for people to specify task knowledge. I also appreciate the authors looking up and citing relevant works from larger AI literature and not just related to Deep RL works. It's also great that the authors try to formalize the language of the space of instructions that will be accepted by the method. With that said, unfortunately, I don’t believe that the paper is quite ready to be accepted for publication yet. My concerns with the paper include a lack of clarity with many technical discussions, missing details, vague and sometimes incorrect claims about the method. All of these factors make it difficult to correctly gauge the technical validity of the approach proposed here. Many of the choices made in terms of techniques or methods used to model and solve the problem aren’t provided any justification and this makes it difficult to understand the work as some of the choices made in the paper run counter to how similar problems are handled in wider literature (for example how you incorporate Finite State Machine transition into state dynamics). Below I have provided a more detailed discussion of my concerns regarding the paper.

Translation to Finite State Machines: First off, the algorithm for generating FSM for a given task specification seems to be missing from the appendix. This is a central part of the paper, as most of the later methods revolve around the choices being made at the level of the finite state machines. Also from a reader’s perspective, the algorithm and related proof of the soundness of construction is important information to have because in general LTL cannot be specified as a Finite State Machines. In the most general case, they require a Buchi automaton, which allows for the acceptance of infinite strings. You can capture finite LTL fragments using FSMs and I assume that’s what’s happening here. I believe the authors must be making an unspecified assumption that the language has some specified upper limit to its task sequences. I didn’t see this mentioned anywhere, nor did it strike me as being true from reading the language description. Additionally, there is an implicit assumption (at least I didn’t see it being explicitly stated anywhere) that each state in the FSM corresponds to an atomic task. Most of the LTL_f translation methods I am familiar with, convert the specification into a non-deterministic finite machine, which is then converted into a deterministic (usually through power-set construction). Just from the few examples provided, I can’t tell that arbitrarily complex task specifications (particularly since language definition allows for recursion) allowed by the task language definition can be represented by an FSM where each FSM state exactly corresponds to an atomic task. I feel without the algorithm and a corresponding proof of correctness, the paper would be incomplete. 

Encoding Finite State Machine: Which brings me to the next point of confusion I had with the paper. Generally, most of the works that augment states of a planning task, with an FSM state do so by encoding the transitions of the FSM into the transition dynamics of the planning problem. This would avoid issues that could happen when the agent just chooses to make some transition even when the transition isn’t warranted. I see that the authors try to add a stop-gap to this problem by including costs to transitions that don't correspond to that skill. But I am confused by the fact why the authors chose to use this formulation, not to mention I can still create pathological scenarios where the agent would force a transition if the probability of the classifiers are just small and not zero (I would be surprised if the learned NLM based classifier assigns zero probability to any of the states). Not only is this a less elegant formulation, but to the best of my understanding, it is this choice that further necessitates the need to use a dynamic programming method in both inverse planning and learning components to figure out what the optimal assignment of FSM states was. Maybe the authors did all this to avoid introducing stochastic transitions (which might come up because of the use of probabilistic classifiers), but I don’t see that as being a major drawback. You could have easily used a probabilistic planner or an MDP solver. I currently don’t think the paper is gaining much from focusing on A* search. 

Inverse Planning: In general, the context in which the term inverse planning is generally used involves the agent recognizing the intention and the goal of another agent (usually a human). This is extremely helpful when you are either planning to assist the agent or in adversarial cases, you are trying to hinder them. In this particular case, it seems the goal is to identify the task after the fact, which I am not sure counts as the whole of inverse planning and I am also not sure it's as useful as being able to identify the agent’s intentions. At the very least, I would recommend clarifying the distinction between what is achieved by the method and the more general case (better yet, use a different term for it). Also, it would be useful to provide some discussion on the utility of such task identification.

Initiation Set for Task and Consecutive Tasks: Is there a reason why the subtasks are characterized by both an initiation set and termination set and not just a subgoal. I understand that this aligns with the traditional view of options, but in this case, is there any advantage one gets from requiring that the transition point corresponds to both the subgoals for the task and the initiation set for the next task. Particularly for fully connected state-space, the initiation set could potentially be extremely large and it would be hard to learn an accurate classifier for that set and which could have negative effects on the planning part as it now introduces potential costs due to inaccurate classifiers. Also at least in the case of A* search, since it's a systematic search, there is no concern of the search getting stuck in a dead-end state.

A* Search and Scalability of the Method: Which brings me to the search part, in particular to the A* search. Multiple parts in the text say that the method could use a learned heuristic and that the search can still identify the optimal solution with some changes to the algorithm. This can’t be true unless the heuristic is admissible. I didn’t see any discussion on how the heuristic was learned and how it was guaranteed to be admissible. There is a note on the evaluation that says “planning in the high-level is currently done with a blind search”, does this mean there is no learned search heuristic? This makes me quite worried about the scalability of the method, as I see no clear way to scale up the methods without learning useful heuristics, which in itself is an open research problem. And without assuming more structure to the problem, I don’t see how you can get more heuristic information. Also, Figure 4 says the max plan length is 4 steps, was this the same throughout all the experiments, these plan lengths are too small to provide any useful evaluation information.

Smaller Comments:

a. One related work that might be worth looking at and also connecting, are the works that use the declarative model to guide the low-level RL agent (examples include [1], [2])

b. It wasn’t clear to me how the discussion about being able to execute multiple tasks at the same time connects with the view of having a state associated with a single FSM state variable corresponding to a task. It might be helpful to provide more information in this regard

c. The composition versus novel task split used in the evaluation, are these only meaningful categories for the baselines? Because after all for the proposed method, as long as the method has learned classifiers for all the atomic tasks, it can be applied to a novel task specification (consisting of a specific formula defined over the tasks are presented). If this is the case, you should clarify it in the evaluation section.

[1] Lyu, Daoming, et al. "SDRL: interpretable and data-efficient deep reinforcement learning leveraging symbolic planning." Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence. Vol. 33. No. 01. 2019.

[2] Yang, Fangkai, et al. "Peorl: Integrating symbolic planning and hierarchical reinforcement learning for robust decision-making." arXiv preprint arXiv:1804.07779 (2018).

There are also some statements, particularly in regards to A* search that seems at the surface to be wrong. I also have some concerns about the scalability of the method.

content.comment:
Thank you for your helpful comments.

**Q1:** Translation to Finite State Machines.

**A:** The language used in this paper covers only a finite fragment of LTL. Specifically, there is no _always_ quantifier in our language, so our fragment does not model task specifications that contain infinite loops.

In the inverse planning experiments (training and inference), negative descriptions are chosen from all descriptions appearing in the dataset (thus the upper limit of the length is 4 during training and 12 during testing). In planning with a black-box test, our search is over sequences up to length 4.

Each node in our FSM corresponds to an atomic skill concept. When constructing FSMs from task descriptions, we didn't directly use non-deterministic finite machines, but used a similar idea of power-set construction to handle "and" connectives. The algorithm is described below, and we have added it to the appendix.

- Recall the definition of FSM on page 4. Each $FSM_t$ is a tuple $(V_t,E_t,VI_t,VG_t)$ which are skill nodes, edges, set of possible starting nodes and set of terminal nodes.
- A single skill $s$ is corresponding FSM with a single node i.e. $VI_t=VG_t=V_t=\{s\}$, and $E_t=\emptyset$.
- $t_1$ **then** $t_2$: we merge $FSM_{t_1}$ and $FSM_{t_2}$ by adding all edges from $VG_{t_1}$ to $VI_{t_2}$. Then, we set $VI_{t_1}$ to be the starting node set and $VG_{t_2}$ to be the terminal node set.
- $t_1$ **or** $\cdots$ **or** $t_n$: Simply merge $n$ FSMs without adding any new edges.
- $t_1$ **and** $\cdots$ **and** $t_n$: build $2^{n-1}n$ sub-FSMs over $n$ layers: the $i$-th layer contains $n\cdot \binom{n-1}{i-1}$ sub-FSMs each labeled by $(s,D)$ where $s$ is the current skill to complete (so this sub-FSM is a copy of $FSM_s$), and $D$ is the set of skills that have been previously completed. Then for a sub-FSM $(s_1,D_1)$ and a sub-FSM $(s_2,D_2)$ in the next layer, if $D_2=D_1\cup\{s_1\}$, we add all edges from terminal nodes of the first sub-FSM to starting nodes of the second sub-FSM. After building layers of sub-FSMs and connecting them, we set the starting nodes to be the union of starting nodes in the first layer and terminal nodes to be the union of terminal nodes in the last layer.
- Note that our framework requires the starting and terminal nodes to be unique, so we introduce the virtual super starting node $v_0$ and terminal node $v_T$.

---

**Q2:** Encoding Finite State Machine.

**A:** Thank you for bringing up this question. We agree that encoding the FSM into the stochastic transition dynamics in the planning domain is another reasonable formulation for encoding the FSM. These two formulations can be unified using a framework of latent transition models, though they are computed using different DP algorithms and may lead to different results. However, transitions with low but non-zero probability may cause issues in both formulations.

First of all, these two formulations are equivalent when the initial/goal classifiers are binary (0/1). When the classifiers are approximated by "soft" functions that indicate the probability they are satisfied, the two formulations correspond to two approaches of integrating reward (i.e. rationality in our model).

The stochastic transition formulation computes the expected rationality, and our formulation can be viewed as an approximation of maximum-likelihood estimated rationality -- we take $\max_\tau \lambda \log \Pr($transitions in $\tau$ are successful$) + Rationality(\bar{s},\bar{a},\tau)$. It would be an interesting extension to adopt the stochastic transition formulation (i.e., $\mathbb{E}_\tau \lambda \log \Pr($transitions in $\tau$ are successful$) + Rationality(\bar{s},\bar{a},\tau)$) and use a stochastic planner or MDP solver, although the planning time might be substantially increased.

Second, even if these two approaches behave differently in some cases, but it is unclear which one is better: this is a fundamental challenge in planning: how should the robot decide whether it has finished a task if there is no indication (such as rewards) from the environment?

We added some discussions regarding this, but the solution to this problem goes beyond the scope of this paper.

---

**Q3:** Inverse Planning.

**A:** We call it inverse planning because we are identifying tasks by inferring the intentions of agents and matching them with the structured skill concepts. Our learned skill concepts are still useful in identifying agents' intentions (i.e. standard inverse planning) before the task is done. This can be done by not forcing the FSM transition computed by the dynamic programming to reach the terminal nodes.

---

Thank you for the detailed responses and for updating the paper. Below are some of my thoughts on the changes/author responses.

Finiteness of the Trace: The always operator in LTL can be defined in terms of the until operator (the authors can just check the Wikipedia entry for LTL) and from what I understand the ‘then’ operator is a stand-in for the until operator. So the author's claim that there can’t be infinite traces due to lack of always operator, doesn’t make total sense to me. I would imagine, you would have to make an explicit assumption about the finiteness of the underlying trace as popularly done in the LTL_f literature [1].

Algorithm: Thank you for adding the algorithm, but as mentioned in my review without a proof sketch of the correctness of the algorithm, I am not sure how to evaluate it. Maybe the correctness of the algorithm is trivially clear for the authors, unfortunately, it wasn’t for me. For example, if you have specifications with repeating tasks like t_1 then ((t_1 and t_2) or (t_1 and t_3)), doesn’t the fact that your algorithm is just doing union over FSM nodes cause issues. It is possible that the current method can handle this case without any issues, but without formal proof, it's unclear to me.

Interleaving: Is the author’s claim that it is interleaving execution because the planner may choose a suboptimal path during an earlier task for the sake of an overall optimal policy? I wouldn’t call this interleaving execution, since as far as the FSM states are considered (which from the framework point of view decides what task is being executed), you are still transitioning between states belonging to the earlier task and none of the latter tasks. I would strongly urge the authors to look for a different term or at least provide a clearer description of this behavior. By the same token, if the planner chooses a more suboptimal policy for a later task to accommodate an earlier one, would you claim that the system is interleaving the execution of the earlier task during the execution of the later one?
 
Inverse Planning: This is again related to the choice of certain terms. As of right now, inverse planning is a rather popular term in certain research communities to refer to a particular problem. From the author's reply, it seems the problem is referred to as inverse planning is not the same problem as what’s more widely known to be inverse planning. I again strongly urge the authors to use a different term to refer to the problem.


[1] G. De Giacomo and M. Vardi, ‘Linear temporal logic and linear dynamic logic on finite traces’, in Proceedings of the Twenty-Fourth International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence, IJCAI’13, pp. 2000–2007. AAAI Press, (2013)

content.comment:
Thank you for your response. We provide our answers to your questions below based on our understanding. Please let us know if you have more questions.

**Q: Finiteness of the Trace.**

**A:** As you inferred, our definition of the task language (on page 4) is based on having finite traces---the definition depends on the trajectory length $n$. So, indeed, the task language we use is actually a fragment of LTL$_f$. Hence, the limitation of finite traces does not come from the lack of the **always** operator, but a direct restriction to LTL$_f$. In LTL$_f$, our **then** can be viewed as the **until** operator. But it's different from the **until** operator in infinite trajectory cases. Thanks for pointing out this possible confusion; we will clarify this in our paper.

**Q: Algorithm.**

**A:** Example: $t_1$ **then** $((t_1$ **and** $t_2)$ **or** $(t_1$ **and** $t_3))$

For the example you provided, the constructed FSM is [here](https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1Zj-ZZj18yZudXFp2PELdePPz27c84wVd), which accurately reflects the semantics of the task description.

Proof: we provide full proof for the construction algorithm, and will add it to our revision.

We want to prove that a trajectory $T$ satisfies the task specification $t$ (described in the formula on page 4) if and only if it can be segmented into a sequence of skills which form a path from the starting node $v_0$ to the terminal node $v_T$ on the FSM constructed by the algorithm provided in Appendix A. (For the proof below, we do not consider the super starting and terminal node $v_0$ and $v_T$; it is easy to incorporate them by adding transition actions before the first action and after the last action in the trajectory. )

- Single skill case is trivial.
- $t_1$ **then** $t_2$.

Consider the edges in $VG_{t_1}\times VI_{t_2}$. They form a cut from all starting nodes $VI_{t_1}$ and terminal nodes $VG_{t_2}$, and it is impossible to go back to $FSM_{t_1}$ after following any of these edges. Hence a valid augmented trajectory will have exactly one transition action corresponding to some edge in $VG_{t_1}\times VI_{t_2}$. This transition action corresponds to a state $s_j$ in the original trajectory, and picking this $s_j$ satisfies the definition in the task language (on page 4), because the transition action will partition the trajectory into two parts, the first of which can match $t_1$ and the second of which can match $t_2$.

In addition, if a trajectory satisfies the definition on page 4, we must have the corresponding $s_j$, so we can insert a transition action corresponding to some edge in  $VG_{t_1}\times VI_{t_2}$ at $s_j$ when augmenting the trajectory. Also, by reduction $s_1\cdots s_j$ matches $FSM_{t_1}$ and $s_j \cdots s_n$ matches $FSM_{t_2}$.

Multiple sub-tasks connected by **then** can be viewed as $(\cdots (t_1$ **then** $t_2)$ **then** $\cdots)$ **then** $t_n)$, and one can apply the proof for binary operator **then**.

- $t_1$ **or** $t_2$.

Clearly, there will be $FSM_{t_1}$ and $FSM_{t_2}$ in the newly constructed FSM in parallel (no intersection). That is, a trajectory matches the FSM if it matches $FSM_{t_1}$ (it can be segmented to sequential skills that form a path on $FSM_{t_1}$) or it matches $FSM_{t_2}$.

- $t_1$ **and** $t_2$ **and** $\cdots$ **and** $t_n$.

By the construction, each path from a starting node to a terminal node form a permutation of $t_1 \cdots t_n$. Hence, if the trajectory can be segmented into sequential sub-tasks that form a permutation of $t_1 \cdots t_n$, it matches a path from a starting node to a terminal node of the FSM.

In the other direction, the trajectory cannot be segmented into sequential sub-tasks that form a permutation of $t_1 \cdots t_n$, it cannot be segmented into any valid path from a starting node to a terminal node on the FSM, and thus it does not match the FSM.


**Q: Interleaving.**

**A:** Thanks for the suggestion. We will change this term to "globally optimal policy". Here, we primarily aim at contrasting our goal-centric representation with policy-based representations.

For example, consider two tasks $t1$ and $t_2$ and the description $t_1$ **then** $t_2$. Consider using policy-based representations: that is, following a policy for $t_1$ until the goal of $t_1$ has been achived, and then execute another policy for $t_2$. In this case, the execution of the policy for $t_1$ is unaware of the execution of $t_2$, which may leads to an overall suboptimal policy. In contrast, our model, while doing planning to achieve the goal for $t_1$ and $t_2$ sequentially, can find the globally optimal policy.

**Q: Inverse Planning.**

**A:** Thanks for your suggestion, we will use the term "plan recognition" instead, which is described in [1] and more similar to our setting.

[1] Ramírez, Miquel, and Hector Geffner. "Plan recognition as planning." Twenty-First International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence. 2009.

**Q4:** Initiation Set ($I_t$) for Consecutive Tasks.

**A:** The learned skill definitions are intended to constitute a hierarchy that is useful both for parsing human activity sequences and efficiently generating behavior. To do so, high-level skills need to account for a bounded interval of activity. Without an explicit understanding of an initiation set, an entire long behavior sequence could conceivably be described just in terms of the final goal condition. For example, picking up an object should be interpreted as from "not holding X" to "holding X", but not as a long sequence of building X from scratch and then picking up it. 

This interpretation agrees with the definition of a broad set of natural language words, such as the representations in [1].

In planning, the initial condition associated with each skill helps limit the horizon when planning for the goal. For example, our planning algorithm will not try to plan for "holding an axe" (the subgoal for skill "pickup-axe") if we haven't yet built an axe (because the initial condition for "pickup-axe" -- having an axe on the ground -- is not satisfied).

Although it is true that the simple planning method we used as a proof-of-concept in this paper does not make use of the initiation sets, more sophisticated planning methods make critical use of preconditions and effects, especially for deriving domain-independent value functions.

---

**Q5:** A* Search and Scalability. Max plan length in Figure 4.

**A:** During training, A* used a neural network-parameterized heuristic function that is trained simultaneously. The heuristic is supervised by the estimated value function computed by Bellman-Ford on the search tree. The heuristic is used to improve search efficiency during training. We didn't use the heuristic for planning, since we don't have a heuristic function trained for unseen tasks, so A* works as a uniform-cost search.  In future work, we would hope to be able to exploit domain-independent planning heuristics on unseen tasks.

In the planning experiments in this paper, as in much of the planning literature, we seek only satisficing plans, which may, indeed, be suboptimal.  As in any planning approach, we can increase the search time to guarantee an optimal solution.

**The "steps" in our planning tasks.** The "4 steps" is the number of skills required to complete the task, and each skill usually requires $6\sim 12$ primitive actions to complete. The 4-step limit only applies to planning with a black-box goal test. Thus, in total, each task requires at most 48 steps. In the case where we plan given a task description, the task descriptions contain up to 14 sequential skills to complete, and some of them take more than 50 primitive actions to complete.

---

[1] Doering, Malcolm. Verb semantics as denoting change of state in the physical world. Michigan State University, 2015.

### Small Comments

**a.** Connecting to SDRL and PEORL.

**A:** SDRL[2] and PEORL[3] relate symbolic planning to (hierarchical) reinforcement learning in order to bring RL better performance, interpretability and data efficiency. Specifically, they align symbolic transitions to options in RL. These approaches, and ours, share the idea of modeling one level of abstraction on actions: i.e., symbolic transitions and skills can both be refined into a sequence of primitive actions. In contrast to these models, which sequentially complete short-term goals by executing policies corresponding to options, RatSkills compose skill concepts into tasks and use a planner to search for solutions.  For this reason, SDRL/PEORL may be more efficient but possibly less flexible at skill execution time. 
In addition, SDRL/PEORL assumes that the semantics of the task/goal descriptions are known in advance, while we are learning them from weakly labeled demonstrations.  They also use this given symbolic vocabulary to describe initiation sets and subgoals, and it is not clear how they could use neural representation to ground these descriptions in sensory (e.g. image) inputs.


**b.** Executing multiple skills at the same time.

**A:** Modeling skill concepts as sub-goals is fundamentally different from executing policies with terminal conditions. Sub-goals allow interleaved execution in some cases. Compared to policies that always focus only on short-term terminal conditions, executing skills aims to minimize the total cost of the task. When planning for two sequential skill concepts, sub-optimal solutions for the first skill are also considered when executing the second skill (those search tree nodes are expanded to the FSM node of the second skill), where they may become optimal because they also make progress toward the goals of skills that appear later on the FSM. Figure 7 provides an example of interleaving skills, where the explicit state transition should happen at the third state (when $s_1$ is completed) but the agent makes progress towards $s_2$ before transiting to the $s_2$ node. The trajectory in figure 7 is an optimal trajectory, and at training time, our A* on the FSM can find it.

**c.** The composition versus novel task split used in the evaluation.

**A:** The *compositional* split contains task descriptions composed of multiple skill concepts, but these same task descriptions have been seen during training. The *novel* split also contains tasks composed of multiple skill concepts (from the same basis set) but the compositions are novel (not seen during training).

After learning the init/goal classifiers, the models that have the temporal structure of skills (BC$_{FSM}$ and RatSkills) can be applied to novel task descriptions. The baselines without such temporal structure can not generalize well to the *novel* split.


[2] Lyu, Daoming, et al. "SDRL: interpretable and data-efficient deep reinforcement learning leveraging symbolic planning." Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence. Vol. 33. No. 01. 2019.

[3] Yang, Fangkai, et al. "Peorl: Integrating symbolic planning and hierarchical reinforcement learning for robust decision-making." arXiv preprint arXiv:1804.07779 (2018).

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a skill-learning framework. As input, the algorithm takes a series of demonstration trajectories $\tau_1, \tau_2, \ldots, \tau_N$, each annotated with corresponding task specifications $t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_N \in \mathcal{T\!L}$ provided in some stuctured language $\mathcal{T\!L}$ (e.g. maybe $t_i = \text{turn-on-music} \textbf{ then } (\text{play-with-ball} \textbf{ or } \text{play-with-monkey})$). Unlike most existing skill-learning work, the resulting skills are represented as option-like subtasks rather than complete policies; in this sense, the skills are "rational" (i.e. correspond to maximising some reward function). This has allows for more flexible skill composition than policy-based representations, and in some environments these goals might also be easier to learn than policies.
content.main_review:
Main strengths of this paper:

- **S1:** The high-level goal—namely, construction of reusable high-level skills from demonstrations—is important to the field, and this approach (particularly the use of structured annotations on demonstrations) is novel so far as I'm aware.
- **S2:** The paper argues well for the use of reward functions rather than policies to define skills. The compositionality advantage (it's easier to interleave achievement of two reward functions than interleave execution of two blackbox policies) particularly resonated.

On the whole, I think this paper would be a valuable addition to the program, which is why I'm leaning "accept". However, I think there are also significant weaknesses to the approach and the way it is presented in the paper:

- **W1:** The experimental evaluation doesn't seem to report performance on the training set. Specifically, Table 1 and Table 2 contain results for the _compositional_ and _novel_ splits, but not for the train split (which I assume is different for the first two). I think this is important for evaluating how well the baselines have actually fit the data; it could be that their poor performance is due to inadequate expressivity or optimisation, and not because of some generalisation failure (e.g. due to lack of compositional structure in the algorithm).
- **W2:** Clarity issues. I could not understand some parts of the method and experimental analysis, as described in the "further requests for clarification" below. There were also some areas where I felt the paper could be reworded for clarity, described in "minor issues and suggestions".
- **W3:** The algorithm must use blind search over tasks when planning without unknown task description $t$. The paper acknowledges this as a weakness.
- **W4:** Parts of the algorithm feel like they could be more principled. e.g. $\mathcal L$ looks a lot like a trajectory log likelihood under a Boltzmann model, but isn't quite a log likelihood (it's not obvious how to fit the task-contrastive term and the $\log G$/$\log I$ terms into a probabilistic generative model). This doesn't influence my score much because it isn't the core conceptual contribution of the paper, but it might be interesting to think about how this framework could be grounded as maximum likelihood (or similar) on a probabilistic model.

Further requests for clarification:

- **CL1:** Section 3: Why is there an explicit initiation condition $I_t$ for each task $t$? $I_t$ could also be left implicit: you could say that any state from which $G_t$ is attainable must satisfy $I_t$.
  
   Indeed, It seems to me that this property is necessary to interleave skills. As an example, say you want to achieve $t = a \textbf{ then } b$. In the course of achieving $G_a = u \land v$, the planner also achieves some prerequisites $p \land q$ to satisfying $G_b = p \land q \land r$. However, this means that $I_b$ needs to be invariant to whether $p$ and $q$ have been satisfied: if $I_b$ is only true when $\neg p$ or $\neg q$ hold, then achieving $G_a$ (and $p \land q$ along the way) is going to make it impossible to initiate the skill for $b$.
  
  If we extend this argument, then it seems that $I_b$ needs to be true for _any_ state along _any_ trajectory that achieves $G_b$, so that the agent can start executing $b$ midway through. But if this is the case, then why not go the whole way and explicitly define $I_b(s)$ as true iff $G_b$ is attainable from $s$?
- **CL2:** Section 4.1: "For planning, we use the built-in deep-Q-learning algorithm." The original maxent IRL does (tabular, exact) soft-value iteration in order to plan. Why is deep Q-learning necessary for these tasks? How does the planner implement the entropy penalty requireed by maxent IRL?
- **CL3:** Section 4.1: "For inverse planning, we rank all candidates by the consistency between the observation and the task-conditioned policy." Why use the policy instead of directly using the return to compare trajectories, given that $p(\overline s, \overline a) \propto \exp R(\overline s, \overline a)$ in the (deterministic) maximum entropy model?
- **CL4:** How does the BC-FSM baseline incorporate an FSM? This was not clear to me from the description in Section 4.1.
- **CL5:** Do the experiments use NLM feature extractors for all baselines, or just for RatSkills? (I think the answer is "yes", just want to double-check.)
- **CL6:** Section A.2: I was quite confused by this description of FSM-A\*, since it does not seem to resemble the description in the appendix. What does it mean to "prune" in A\*? Why is this pruning only applied after the first $b$ layers? Psuedocode may be useful here.

Minor issues and suggestions:

- **M1:** When I saw "abstract language descriptions" in the abstract, I assumed the paper was going to focus on _natural_ language. It wasn't until I got to page 4 that I understood that it was referring to a structured, logical language. This could be clarified by referring to rephrasing slightly, such as by calling them "abstract logical descriptions", or by making the given example look more formal, which is what I tried to do above by writing, e.g., $\text{turn-on-music}$ instead of "turn on music" (the current underlining in the abstract helps but was not sufficient for me to intuit the structure of the language).
- **M2:** In Section 3.3, the description of A\* refers to the priority used to pop nodes from the priority queue as a "heuristic function" ("Each node is associated with a heuristic value which adds up the total cost of the agent reaching this state and an estimated cost-to-go"). This is a bit weird; in the planning community, a "heuristic" is generally something that estimates cost-to-go. I'd recommend stealing terms from Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, which calls the combined function an "evaluation function" $f(n) = g(n) + h(n)$, which is  the sum of the "path cost" $g(n)$ and the "heuristic value" $h(n)$.
- **M3:** While reading the "task language" section, I assumed "primitive skills" were the same thing as "primitive actions". It seems like this isn't the case; atomic skills in the task language exist at a strictly more abstract level than primitive actions from the MDP. I recommend exclusively referring to these as "atomic skills" or similar, and reserving "primitive" only for actions in the base-level MDP (which I think is typical nomenclature in hierarchial RL).
- **M4:** Section 4.2: the appendix notes that the Crafting World environment has been modified relative to that used in past work. The fact that the experiments use a modified environment should be mentioned in the body of the paper, and the changes should be explicitly justified in the appendix.
- **M5:** Appendix A.2: the sub-section which discusses optimality of A\* search should also note that the heuristic must be admissible in order to guarantee optimal solutions (this will typically not be the case for learned heuristics).

Although I'm convinced of the significance of this work, I was confused by some important details, particularly regarding the experiments. I would like to have these clarified so that I can increase my score (and confidence). I also think that some of the wording could be slightly rejigged for clarity, although this was not as big a factor in my rating.

content.comment:
Thank you for your helpful comments.

**W1:** Performance on the training set.

**A:** Our training is on the inverse planning problem, and we report the training accuracy on the compositional tasks in the training set.


| Model | Crafting World | | Playroom |  |
| -------- | -------- | -------- |-------- | -------- |
| *Split=Com.* |  Train Acc. | Test Acc.  |      Train Acc. | Test Acc.    |
|LSTM| $99.8\%$ | $100.0\%$ | $95.6\%$ | $51.1\%$ |
| IRL     | $70.5\%$ | $64.1\%$   | $85.8\%$ | $92.5\%$     |
| BC     | $99.6\%$ | $85.6\%$     | $95.3\%$ | $72.5\%$     |
| BC-FSM(Ours)     | $100.0\%$ | $100.0\%$     | $91.9\%$ | $85.0\%$     |
| RatSkills(Ours)     | $99.7\%$ | $97.2\%$     | $99.1\%$ | $97.5\%$     |



We can see that for compositional tasks that are used both in training and testing, the Behavior Cloning (without FSM) baseline can accurately fit the training data but experiences some performance drop when testing. The IRL baseline performs comparatively poorly on both training and testing, suggesting that the lack of compositional structure hinders both expressivity and generalization.  Importantly, Behavior Cloning and IRL experience a significant performance drop from the compositional split (seen) to the novel split (unseen), which indicates the compositional structure is crucial for generalization to novel tasks.


---

**W2:** Clarity issues.

**A:** Thanks for your suggestions, we will fix them in our revision.

---

**W3:** Blind search when planning without known task description $t$.

**A:** It is true that our proof-of-concept planner assumes that the task can be completed within a short sequence of skills, and thus a blind/enumerative search at the skill level can work.

However, learned skills still improve the efficiency even for the enumerative search. A theoretical justification is included in Appendix A.2.


---

**W4:** How can RatSkills be grounded on a probabilistic model.

**A:** The rationality score consists of two parts: the likelihood of a rational agent choosing the given trajectory (under the Boltzmann model), and the likelihood all transitions are valid (the corresponding initial and goal conditions are satisfied). In principle, the likelihood under the Boltzmann model is sufficient for learning skill representations. 

However, the rationality is computed based on $J_t$ which is estimated by A* and may not be good enough at the early state of learning, especially when the agent is far from completing the task. In practice, adding the initial/goal terms does help the model learn, and it is still a meaningful formulation with these terms:  we are optimizing $\max_{\text{seg}}\lambda\log \Pr(\text{seg}|\bar{s},\bar{a})+\text{Reward}(\bar{s},\bar{a}, \text{seg})$, where $\text{seg}$ is a segmentation of the trajectory into tasks, and $\text{Reward}$ is based on rationality ($Rat$ in our paper).

We have run an ablation study using the score without the transition probability terms; i.e., $I_t$ and $G_t$. On the compositional split of the crafting world, RatSkills experiences difficulty during learning: we got $27.5\%$ accuracy on inverse planning problem, and $14.5\%$ accuracy on planning. 

---

Thank you to the authors for their comprehensive response. I have a similar overall assessment to when I was writing the review: the author response addressed most of my concerns, but there were also a couple of significant parts that I feel it did not address, and one additional significant concern from reviewer sPaL about soundness and clarity of the FSM construction. I'm still weakly in favour of acceptance despite these issues, but agree with other reviewers that the paper could benefit from more clarity in the methods section. I'll respond in more detail in the order that points were raised above.

**W1:** Thanks for including results in the train split too! I'm a bit concerned that the patterns in baseline behaviour are so different across the two environments. e.g. why does LSTM get perfect test accuracy in Crafting World, but suffer a 46% drop in accuracy between train and test in Playroom? Why does non-hierarchical IRL do better on the test set than on the train set in Playroom? etc. This concern could be addressed by running experiments on more domains to get a better sense of how often RatSkills actually provides value (although adding domains is hard, and I don't see this as a make-or-break issue).

**W2:** Resolved.

**W3:** This justification seems reasonable—I accept that the method can plan more efficienctly even with blind search at the top level, so long as primitives are chosen correctly.

**W4:** I'm not convinced by the claim that $\sum_{\substack{a'=(v,v')\in\overline{a}'} \\\\ \text{is an FSM transition}} \left[\log G_v(s_i) + \log I_{v'}(s_i) \right]$ is the log probability of a task segmentation. As I understand it, $G_v$ and $I_{v'}$ parameterise a Bernoulli random variable indicating whether a task ends or starts at the given state, respectively. There doesn't seem to be any architectural constraint ensuring that the joint distribution is normalised, though—e.g. we could have $I_v(s)=1$ and $G_v(s)=1$ for all $v, s$, in which case every segmentation will have probability 1.

**CL1:** Resolved.

**CL2-3:** I understand what is being done here now—the algorithm is doing "hard" Q-learning (as opposed to soft value iteration, like MCE IRL), then taking a softmax over the Q-values. I think this is fine, but it's worth noting somewhere in the paper that it's not the same thing as maxent IRL. Specifically, the policy being proposed in this paper is the solution to the following equations (in a finite-horizon environment)

$$\\begin{align*}
Q^{\\text{hard}}_T(s,a) &= r(s,a) \\\\
V^{\\text{hard}}_t(s) &= \\max_a Q^{\\text{hard}}_t(s,a) \\\\
Q^{\\text{hard}}_t(s,a) &= r(s,a) + \\mathbb E V^{\\text{hard}}(s')\\\\
\\pi_t^{\\text{hard}}(a \\mid s) &\\propto \\exp Q_t^{\\text{hard}}(s,a)~,
\\end{align*}$$

($\\mathbb E V^{\\text{hard}}(s')$ should be $\\mathbb E_{s' \\sim \\mathcal T} V_{t+1}^{\\text{hard}}(s')$; OpenReview just won't render it properly)

whereas the maximum (causal) entropy IRL policy would be the solution to

$$\begin{align*}
Q_T(s,a) &= r(s,a) \\\\
V_t(s) &= \log \sum_a \exp Q_t(s,a) \\\\
Q_t(s,a) &= r(s,a) + \mathbb E_{s' \sim \mathcal T} V_{t+1}(s') \\\\
\pi_t^{\text{soft}}(a \mid s) &\propto \exp Q_t^\text{soft}(s,a)~.
\end{align*}$$

which will in general not yield the same policy $\pi$.

**CL5-6:** Resolved.

**Other reviewers' concerns:** I'd like to echo reviewer sPaL's concern that the FSM construction. In particular, what happens when the same skill appears in several places in a task specification? Is a separate initiation and goal classifier learnt for each instance of the skill? (which seems to be implied by the definition of the cost function at the bottom of page 4, which associates initiation/goal classifiers with vertices in the FSM, rather than skills)

content.title: Author Response to Reviewer B9ia - part 2
content.comment:
**CL1:** Why is there an explicit $I_t$?

The learned skill definitions are intended to constitute a hierarchy that is useful both for parsing human activity sequences and efficiently generating behavior. To do so, high-level skills need to account for a bounded interval of activity. Without an explicit understanding of an initiation set, an entire long behavior sequence could conceivably be described just in terms of the final goal condition. For example, picking up an object should be interpreted as from "not holding X" to "holding X", but not as a long sequence of building X from scratch and then picking up it. 

This interpretation agrees with the definition of a broad set of natural language words, such as the representations in [1].

In planning, the initial condition associated with each skill helps limit the horizon when planning for the goal. For example, our planning algorithm will not try to plan for "holding an axe" (the subgoal for skill "pickup-axe") if we haven't yet built an axe (because the initial condition for "pickup-axe" -- having an axe on the ground -- is not satisfied).

Although it is true that the simple planning method we used as a proof-of-concept in this paper does not make use of the initiation sets, more sophisticated planning methods make critical use of preconditions and effects, especially for deriving domain-independent value functions.


---

**CL2:** Deep-Q-learning algorithm and implementation of MaxEnt IRL.

**A:** The soft-value iteration algorithm cannot be run on the domain due to the huge space (much more than $10^9$). Therefore, we use a deep-Q-network to realize the value/reward function on the state space.

---

**CL3:** MaxEnt IRL on Inverse planning.

**A3:** Thanks for your suggestion. In principle, using trajectory probability and reward should be equivalent. In practice, we use deep-Q-learning to approximate the Q function based on the reward function, and the policy is computed from the Boltzmann distribution based on the Q function. Hence, the policy is differentiable with respect to the Q function but not directly with respect to the reward function, so we expect that the optimization would be less effective using that strategy.

We tried to use reward function rather than trajectory probability and got $39.5\%$ ($\leftarrow 64.1\%$) accuracy for inverse planning and $42.1\%$ ($\leftarrow 36.5\%$) success rate for planning on the *compositional* split in Crafting World.

---

**CL4:** How does BC-FSM incorporate an FSM?

**A:** The BC-FSM model learns skill-conditioned policies as well as a termination condition for each skill. For the inverse planning task, we first compute the policy at each step of the trajectory for each node in the FSM (the policy is conditioned on the FSM node), and then use dynamic programming to find a segmentation that maximizes the overall likelihood of the trajectory based on the conditional policy (i.e., the likelihood of taking the stop action at each FSM transition is also included). For the planning task, we try all possible paths from the start nodes to the terminal nodes on the FSM, and sequentially run skills along the path. Among the paths, we report the one with maximum overall likelihood. Details can be found in Appendix C.4.

---

**CL5:** Are NLM features used in all baselines?

**A:** Yes.

---

**CL6:** "Prune" FSM-A*.

**A:** In our implementation, we first run $b$ layers of Breadth-First-Search from the root and then run A* from the leaves. This is to prevent an imperfectly learned heuristic from misleading the A* search at the beginning (all possible trajectories in the first $b$ steps are enforced to be explored). We have updated Appendix A.2.

---

**M1-M5:** We have revised our paper accordingly.

[1] Doering, Malcolm. Verb semantics as denoting change of state in the physical world. Michigan State University, 2015.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a framework for learning how to perform a collection of tasks (encoding acyclic state machines) in a fixed (deterministic) workspace. Importantly, the guards/transition symbols that the task is defined over, is apriori unknown. The key contribution of this work is to simultaneously learn classifiers to map world states to task symbols and create an agent that can perform the tasks in the workspace.
content.main_review:
The key contribution of this work seems to be in grounding the symbols of the task description using a collection of (task, demonstration) pairs and variant of Boltzmann rationality, as per [1], and a custom mapping from task to reward function. Once grounded,  the paper describes using classic planning (A*) techniques for achieving that task. Unsurprisingly, once grounded, the Ratskills framework is able to perform extremely well since the dynamics are fairly simple/deterministic and the tasks are a short sequence of reach problems - which A* is known to be well equipped to handle.

The particular contrastive  approach suggested for grounding is interesting, and I have not seen it used for grounding tokens in formal languages (although this is outside my area of expertise). This addresses a common criticism of formal controller synthesis, which requires grounding the predicates for planning.

I have three concerns with the paper:

My primary concern with the paper is with the baselines. For example in the crafting domain, did IRL get access to the state 260 state features? Was the classic MaxEnt RL algorithm (e.g., no deep learning) run on those features? Maybe this is mis-guided, but it seems that no deep learning is required to run MaxEnt RL for this domain and may perform better? 

My secondary concern is generalizing to stochastic transition models and/or partial observability, where A* may prove an insufficient planner. Perhaps the proposed approach could be combined with the hierarchical planning considered in [2]?

Finally, I am concerned about the scalability of the enumerative approach to search for tasks to connect to the demonstrations. While sufficient for the very restricted concept class presented, this could be a concern when generalizing to more expressive task domains.

------
Typos and small concerns:
1. The task classifiers, G, are used as both [0, 1] and {0, 1} valued variables. Could this abuse of notation be made explicit?
2. The the context of Boltzmann rational models, the inverse temperature is often called the rationality, which is slightly confusing in this context.
3. The paragraph before experiments seems to contain several typos (e.g., we use compute).

content.title: General Response to Reviewers
content.comment:
We thank all reviewers for their insightful reviews and helpful suggestions. In our overall statement, we would like to reiterate the motivation and the problem formulation of our model: why do we need skill concepts, and why is the proposed representation useful?

**Learning skill concepts for planning.** Being able to decompose complex tasks into sub-goals can help long-term planning. For example, planning to go across the river "from scratch" is hard, as it requires a long-term plan going from building tools to crafting boats, but it can be made easier if we know that "having an axe", "having wood", and "having a boat" are useful sub-goals. Planning hierarchically with these subgoals can substantially reduce the search required.

It is also helpful if we have knowledge about when a subgoal can be easily achieved: knowing that crafting boats needs the initial condition of having wood is useful because we can further decompose the subgoal of "having a boat" into two stages: "collecting wood" and "crafting boat". 

*Learning* useful subgoals and their initial conditions (i.e., a skill concept as a whole) from data is important but very hard without any supervision. In this paper, we propose to learn them from a small amount of very weak human supervision.

**Learning skill concepts for communication.** Another important application of skill concept learning is to create a language interface for human-robot communication. This involves both robots interpreting human actions and humans instructing robots by specifying a sequence of skill concepts to execute. Here, learning a goal-centric representation enables compositional generalization through flexible composition of learned skill concepts. This general ability can be applied temporally to interpret novel action sequences and execute novel instructions.

Our main contribution in this paper is a novel framework for learning skill concepts (i.e., paired initial conditions and subgoals) from paired human-generated descriptions and rational demonstrations. We assume that humans are rational, so that the demonstration can be decomposed into segments and each segment corresponds to a rational trajectory towards a subgoal. Our algorithm jointly solves the segmentation and the initial/goal condition learning problem.
